item.research_question: Can the dawsonite-type structure (NH4M(OH)2CO3) adapt to a high-entropy form incorporating five or more cations with equimolar and homogeneous distribution?
item.material_system: High-entropy dawsonite-type structures with a base of Al, Fe, Cr, Ga and a fifth cation varied by ionic radius (In, Er, Ho, Y, Eu, Ce, La); reference single-cation Al-Dawsonite (Al)
item.processing_route: Coprecipitation: Metal nitrate solution (9 mmol total in 40 mL water) added dropwise (6 mL/min) to ammonium bicarbonate solution (0.06 mol in 75 mL water, pH adjusted to 9.5 with NH4OH); stirred overnight (~20 h) at room temperature; centrifuged and dried overnight at 333 K
item.test_conditions: XRD (Cu Kα, 2θ range); SEM/EDX (20 kV); HAADF-STEM (300 kV); TGA (up to 600 °C, 10 °C/min, synthetic air); FTIR (320–4000 cm–1); N2 adsorption (77 K, degassed at 373 K); Calcination at 523 K; Reconstruction in 1 M (NH4)2CO3 at 323 K
key_findings: All high-entropy samples (In, Er, Ho, Y, Ce as fifth cation) showed characteristic dawsonite reflections at 2θ = 15.4°, 26.9°, and 35.1° with no additional phases observed.
EDS mapping confirmed homogeneous distribution of the five cations (In, Al, Fe, Cr, Ga) throughout the particles.
FTIR analysis showed a red-shift of the vOH band from 3434 cm–1 (Al-Daw) to ~3345 cm–1 in multicationic materials.
Thermogravimetric analysis indicated only a 4–8% difference between observed and calculated weight loss, suggesting small amounts of amorphous phase.
High-entropy samples exhibited Type II N2 isotherms, whereas the Al-Daw reference showed a Type IV isotherm with H1 hysteresis.
The high-entropy sample In-AlFeCrGa maintained a specific surface area of 314 m2/g, which increased to 373 m2/g after reconstruction.
Full reconstruction of the dawsonite structure was achieved after calcination at 523 K followed by treatment with ammonium carbonate.
Pure dawsonite-type structures were formed with lanthanides (Ho, Ce, Er) which previously were difficult to incorporate due to mutually exclusive pH regimes.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the structural stability and cation incorporation to the flexibility of the dawsonite-type lattice, noting that the 'many-interaction situation arising from the cation mix and lattice distortions' leads to observed spectral shifts. The memory effect is explained by the ability of the amorphous phase formed at 523 K to completely reconstruct the crystalline dawsonite structure upon exposure to ammonium carbonate solution.
item.limitations: The materials are not stable at high temperatures due to their hydrated nature, meaning they may not qualify as 'entropy-stabilized' under certain definitions. Additionally, the high-resolution STEM imaging caused sensitive damage to the multicationic material.
item.future_work: The authors hypothesize that high-entropy dawsonite-type structures are even more versatile in cation incorporation than demonstrated and suggest that 'under optimized synthesis conditions for specific elements of interest, a wide range of chemistry can be obtained in the high-entropy form.'
quotes: Through a coprecipitation synthesis method, dawsonite-type materials readily took a high-entropy form with five cations that were equimolar and homogeneously distributed.
Specifically, the vOH at 3434 cm–1 is red-shifted to ∼ 3345 cm–1 for all multicationic materials, which could indicate the strengthening of the hydrogen bond interaction.
After treatment with ammonium carbonate, the crystallinity again completely recovered.
